evidence.text:
Simplified form of 學.  Originally composed of the numbers five (㐅) and six (六), representing study of arithmetic. 
Later two hands (又) were added on the left and right side of the character, possibly depicting counting with fingers or hands-on teaching.
Finally a child (子) was added to the bottom, depicting a child being educated.
The bottom part of 六 (six) was reanalyzed as 宀 (roof) and interpreted as a building for learning.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Possibly a phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɡruːɡ): phonetic 爻 (OC *ɢraːw) + phonetic 六 (OC *ruɡ). Later, 𦥑 was added to form 𦥯, and a semantic 子 (“child”) was added for differentiation.
Another explanation is abbreviated 敎 (“to teach”) + 𦥑 (“mingling hands; hands-on learning”) + 宀 (“house; roofed building”) – a child learning in a roofed place. However, the oracle bone script does not include a child.
In the modern form, 六 has corrupted to 冖 (“cover”), and the hands 𦥑 around the 爻 have become connected with the 冖. Shuowen regards 𦥑 as the phonetic component in the character, which may be true according to some Old Chinese reconstructions such as that of Pan Wuyun's, though probably not others.
See also the top component of 覺, which is a contraction of 學.
Endopassive/volitional derivation of 覺 (OC *kruːɡ, “to become aware”) (Sagart, 2004; Schuessler, 2007; Baxter and Sagart, 2014). Ultimately from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *kruk (“to rouse; to awaken; to disturb”).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨、金文、簡帛用例
evidence.text: The database reports oracle-bone forms of 學 and interprets them as hands manipulating counting or divination tallies, with 五 and 六 in some forms and 爻 in others. It proposes learning as the early sense, while also recording an alternative analysis in which 爻 is phonetic. The account says bronze forms add 子. It cites an oracle-bone occurrence in 《屯南》60, 于大學尋, and bronze occurrences including 大盂鼎’s 余唯即朕小學 and 靜簋’s learning/teaching archery passage. It also reports the Qin Shuihudi slip phrase 成學, “complete one’s studies,” and a Han-slip loan use of 學 for 覺, “feel/perceive.” These are source-reported readings and examples; the proposed tally interpretation is not uncontested.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 學

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨文構形分析
evidence.text: The source describes 𦥑 as depicting two hands and identifies 五, 六, and sometimes 爻 in the oracle-bone graph. Separately, its 爻 entry reports oracle-bone use for divination, a separate possible depiction involving tally slips, and an oracle-bone use of 爻 read as 學 in a personal name. Thus, an early sound association between the graphs is reported, but this does not by itself establish that 爻 was a phonetic component in every form of 學. The source’s modern pronunciation display for 爻 offers yáo and xiáo readings; this is not ancient phonological evidence.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 學

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 《說文》 account and later usage chronology
evidence.text: The entry quotes the Shuowen account: 斆 is “to awaken/enlighten,” formed from 教 and 冖, with 𦥑 as phonetic; 學 is an abbreviated seal-script form of 斆. The entry also cites the Classic of Poetry line 日就月將，學有緝熙于光明, bronze-inscription uses for school and instruction, and the Qin slip 成學. It notes a Han-slip occurrence where 學 is read as 覺 in the sense “feel/perceive.” The attested extension from learning to school/instruction and the distinct Han loan spelling should be kept separate from the graphic-origin account.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 學

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解; competing construction account
evidence.text: The database also records a proposal attributed to Shirakawa Shizuka: 學 from 爻 and 宀, depicting crossed roof timbers and a school building. The database presents this as an alternative explanation, not its main analysis. The visible modern top ⺍/冖 should not be taken as direct evidence for a roof or building in the ancient graph; the oracle-bone and bronze forms are separately catalogued, and no glyph image was visually inspected for this report.

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart
evidence.text: The 2014 Baxter–Sagart table lists 爻 yáo, Middle Chinese haew, Old Chinese *N-kˤraw, gloss “change; hexagram.” This is the exact 爻 row inspected in that reconstruction system.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (20 September 2014)

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart
evidence.text: The 2014 Baxter–Sagart table lists 學 xué, Middle Chinese haewk, Old Chinese *m-kˤruk, gloss “study; imitate.” Compared with the separately inspected 爻 row (*N-kˤraw), the forms differ in initial and rhyme material. This comparison alone does not rule out a historically conditioned or restricted phonetic role for 爻 in some early spellings; it does not establish a simple matching sound value.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (20 September 2014)

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, 香港中文大學
evidence.field: 子: received form and script examples
evidence.text: The entry identifies 子 and displays oracle-bone and bronze examples; it quotes 說文 treating 子 as an象形 graph. CUHK’s 學 entry reports 子 added in bronze forms in its analysis. The child interpretation within 學 is that source’s analysis, not an explanation of current 学 as a whole.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 子

evidence.source: 白川静 account as reported by CUHK; publication itself not inspected
evidence.text: CUHK attributes to Shirakawa Shizuka an alternative reading of 學 as 爻 plus 宀, with crossed roof timbers and a school building. CUHK presents it as an alternative to the hands-and-tallies account. Shirakawa’s underlying publication was not inspected, so this is a report of CUHK’s attribution, not direct verification of the original argument.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 學

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, 香港中文大學
evidence.field: 學: 說文 quotation and later usage examples
evidence.text: CUHK quotes 說文’s account that 斆 means 覺悟, is analyzed from 教 and 冖 with 𦥑聲, and that 學 is an abbreviated seal-script form of 斆. It separately reports 學 used for learning in oracle-bone evidence, school and archery instruction in bronze inscriptions, 成學 (“complete studies”) on Qin slips, and 學 used as a loan graph for 覺 (“feel/perceive”) in Han slips. These examples do not establish a complete semantic chronology; the Han loan spelling is separate from graphic formation and from the ordinary learning sense.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 學

evidence.source: 精選版 日本国語大辞典 via コトバンク
evidence.text: The dictionary records がく for learning, instruction received, and knowledge, citing 「皆令就学」 in 続日本紀, dated 718. It also gives an organized system of knowledge as a later attested sense, with a cited example from 1917. This Japanese lexical evidence does not establish a continuous semantic path from ancient Chinese uses.
evidence.title: 学(ガク)とは？ 意味や使い方 - コトバンク

evidence.source: 精選版 日本国語大辞典 via コトバンク
evidence.field: 学ぶ: readings, senses, dated examples
evidence.text: The entry records 学ぶ まなぶ with senses including imitating, learning from instruction, and studying. Examples include まなぶ in 枕草子 (late 10th century), 源氏物語 (1001–14), and an 883 annotated Buddhist text. These attestations document Japanese word use, not the origin of the Chinese graph.
evidence.title: 学ぶ(マナブ)とは？ 意味や使い方 - コトバンク

evidence.source: 公益財団法人 日本漢字能力検定協会, 漢字ペディア
evidence.field: 学: current Japanese readings, meanings, and compounds
evidence.text: The entry lists ガク and まなぶ, meanings including learning, organized knowledge, and school, and compounds such as 学校 (がっこう) and 学習 (がくしゅう). Its cited examples support these as Japanese uses; the on-reading and kun-reading should not be conflated.
evidence.title: 学 | 漢字一字 | 漢字ペディア

evidence.source: Kotobank, 精選版 日本国語大辞典
evidence.field: 学ぶ: exact kun-reading lexical example
evidence.text: The dictionary records 学ぶ as まなぶ, with examples for imitating, learning from instruction, and studying. This supports 学ぶ（まなぶ）as a beginner-useful kun-reading example.
evidence.title: 学ぶ(マナブ)とは？ 意味や使い方 - コトバンク

evidence.source: Kotobank, 精選版 日本国語大辞典
evidence.text: The dictionary gives 学 (がく) for learning or study and records the dated example 「皆令就学」 from 718. Kanjipedia also lists ガク and meanings of learning, school, and organized knowledge.
evidence.title: 学(ガク)とは？ 意味や使い方 - コトバンク

evidence.source: 国立国語研究所, ことば研究館
evidence.field: Japanese form history: 新字体 and 旧字体
evidence.text: The institute explains that the 1949 当用漢字字体表 prescribed simplified forms including 新字体, and that these were carried into the 1981 常用漢字表. This general account supports the Japanese standardization context for 新字体 and 旧字体; the specific pairing 学/學 is directly shown by Kanjipedia’s 学 entry.
evidence.title: 「国」と「國」のように、昔と今とで形がちがう漢字があるのはなぜですか

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 學/学 relation and documentary history of simplified shape
evidence.text: The 学 variant record under 學 says the shape developed from running-cursive writing regularized into standard form, identifies it as a simplified form/variant of 學, and cites its inclusion in a 1935 Ministry simplified-character table. This is evidence about the character’s variant history in that source’s Chinese lexicographic context; it does not establish that the Japanese and mainland Chinese reforms followed identical processes.
evidence.title: 學 — Ministry of Education《Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants》

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart
evidence.field: Book publication and Old Chinese methodology context
evidence.text: Oxford Academic identifies William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart, Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction, Oxford University Press, published 30 September 2014. The table rows inspected for 學 and 爻 are in their downloadable 2014 reconstruction materials; those system-specific reconstructions are analyses, not direct recordings of ancient pronunciation.
evidence.title: Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction

evidence.source: Unicode Consortium
evidence.field: Unihan lookup documentation and exact character lookup attempts
evidence.text: Unicode’s Unihan documentation describes the interface for individual ideograph properties. Direct lookups for 学 U+5B66, 學 U+5B78, 子 U+5B50, 爻 U+723B, and 𦥑 U+26951 failed in this session. The packet’s local kMandarin rows report xué for 学 and 學, yáo for 爻, and jú for 𦥑; these are local data only and no exact official character page verifying them was inspected. The B–S reconstruction table lists 爻 yáo and 學 xué in its Mandarin field, but that is not an official Unihan citation.

evidence.text: The page identifies 子 as the radical and describes the visible current graph as an upper abbreviated shape over 子, naming upper shapes ⺍ and 冖. This supplies a visible-shape description, not evidence that the current upper forms retain independent ancient semantic roles. It is a secondary character-reference site and its historical construction narrative conflicts in details with Kanjipedia and CUHK.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

etymology_notes.text: A building 冖 where children 子 study; ⺍ provides the pronunciation

Simplified form of 學.  Originally composed of the numbers five (㐅) and six (六), representing study of arithmetic. 
Later two hands (又) were added on the left and right side of the character, possibly depicting counting with fingers or hands-on teaching.
Finally a child (子) was added to the bottom, depicting a child being educated.
The bottom part of 六 (six) was reanalyzed as 宀 (roof) and interpreted as a building for learning.

context.japanese_editorial_instructions:
Write an English-language etymology entry for a JAPANESE learner, about the
Japanese graph named in this dossier. The historical graph may originate in China, but current
Japanese readings and senses are separate research questions. The source_reuse packet is a
reviewed prior Chinese research starting point, not an approved Japanese article. Consult local
sources AND external Japanese dictionary references; verify citations before transferring claims.
Use authoritative Japanese dictionaries (Kanjipedia, KANJIDIC2/JMdict, scholarly sources) for
Japanese readings and senses, and Cultural Affairs form tables for documented form conventions.
Write independently. Reuse supported historical facts, source records and exact-graph glyphs;
do not transfer modern Chinese usage, meaning history, Mandarin learner sound comparisons or
components from a different graph. Inspect prior_analysis as a lead and correct it where needed.
For shinjitai, distinguish the Japanese current form, kyujitai, and simplified Chinese; similarity
alone is not proof of shared reform history. A counterpart's images remain explicitly scoped to
that counterpart. Do not infer a Japanese-created character merely from its absence in Chinese.
Learner overview starts with useful Japanese meaning and a sourced logical current component
split. Keep ancient Chinese sound roles separate from Japanese on/kun readings. A Chinese
phonetic role need not predict a kun reading. If comparing Japanese on readings, provide supported
component and host readings; matching current readings alone do not prove historical phonetic
formation. Mandarin comparisons belong only in clearly labeled expert historical context when
actually useful, never as the Japanese learner default.
Include language="ja" and japanese_usage: summary plus 2-4 selected reading records (1 if only
one useful reading is supported), with type on/kun/special, reading in kana, an actual example
containing the entry graph, full example_reading in kana, a concise English gloss, and explanation.
Examples and readings require inspected Japanese lexical evidence, not invented combinations.
Prefer beginner-useful examples; do not claim JLPT membership of an example without evidence.
Kun dictionary dots mark okurigana, not literal spelling. Special readings such as jukujikun
belong to whole words and must not be assigned mechanically to individual components. Explain
multiple readings briefly without dumping all dictionary readings or nanori. Cite usage and
reading claims. On readings are historically borrowed; kun readings associate Japanese words
with the graph, not Chinese pronunciations. State only source-supported transmission details.
Meaning_history distinguishes early graph/Chinese word history from established Japanese uses;
do not invent a continuous semantic path between them. Inspect Japanese attestations where
available and record gaps. Write neutral reader prose; bibliography specifics stay in citations.
Reviewers must evaluate the Japanese adaptation, lexical examples, form scopes, reuse provenance
and all ordinary factual/readability gates independently. An approved Chinese entry is not a
Japanese approval.

gaps: No inspected authoritative Japanese source gives a semantic explanation for the current upper abbreviation of 学. Describe the learner split as visible upper abbreviated shape plus 子, and do not assign the historical 本字 analysis to current 学.

The specific printed passage and page in 角川新字源 改訂新版 cited by Kanjipedia were not independently opened; page number and edition-specific pagination remain unavailable. Kanjipedia itself was inspected and attributes the account to that edition.

The exact graphic path from early oracle-bone 學 through later forms to Japanese 学 is not resolved by the inspected sources. The Taiwan Ministry variant dictionary documents a cursive-to-regularized account and an older table, but that does not by itself document every stage of the Japanese standardization history.

The Shirakawa analysis is known here through CUHK’s attribution only; the underlying publication was not inspected. The competing tally account also remains a source analysis, not a settled original referent.

A possible sound role for 爻 in some early forms is reported by CUHK, but its local Baxter–Sagart comparison with 學 shows *N-kˤraw versus *m-kˤruk. The evidence inspected here does not establish the precise phonological mechanism or its applicability to every early form.

An exact early pronunciation or original name for any depicted tally/object in the proposed borrowing or pictorial analyses was not independently recovered. The account of 爻 as tally-like divination pieces is itself an etymological proposal, not independent proof of their ancient spoken name.

CUHK reports oracle-bone, bronze, Qin-slip, and Han-slip examples, but artifact catalogues and narrow archaeological dates for those cited examples were not independently checked in this pass. These examples do not establish a complete semantic chronology.

The reported Han-slip use of 學 for 覺 is a graph-borrowing use distinct from graphic development and the ordinary learning sense. Its complete phonological pathway and earlier occurrence were not verified.

Official Unihan individual character pages for 학 etc. failed; exact local current-reading rows are available in the supplied packet but no external Unicode record was inspectable. Unicode general documentation is not a substitute for those exact readings.

summary.text: 学 is the standardized simplified form of 學, the character used for learning and study. Competing accounts explain the early construction of 學; the modern simplified shape does not resolve them.

formation.text: The early construction discussed here is that of 學. One account describes two hands, 𦥑, manipulating tally-like marks, with 五 and 六 in some forms and 爻 in others; it allows that 爻 may have supplied a sound cue in some forms. A distinct proposal reads 爻 with 宀 as crossed roof timbers and a school building. These analyses remain disputed, and the modern form 学 does not determine which, if either, explains every early graph.

history.text: The selected early-style image is a modern vector tracing identified as an oracle-bone-style form of 學. It shows crossing upper strokes and a broad curved lower form, but those features do not decide between the reported interpretations.
學 is the traditional counterpart of standardized simplified 学. The graphic path from early forms to either modern shape is not established here.

A later lexicographic account describes 學 as an abbreviated seal-script form of 斆, which it analyzes as 教 and 冖 with 𦥑 supplying the sound. This received account does not confirm the structure of earlier forms.

uncertainties.text: The hands-and-tallies interpretation, a possible sound role for 爻 in some forms, and the alternative 爻-plus-宀 interpretation are distinct competing accounts; none is established for every early form.
The graphic path from early 學 forms to 学 is unresolved. The modern top alone does not establish an ancient roof component or a specific corruption.
An oracle-bone occurrence is reported, but its archaeological date and context are not specified beyond that identification.

senses.text: An oracle-bone occurrence is reported, and learning is identified as an early sense. This is an early documented use, not necessarily the graph’s original meaning.
Bronze-inscription examples are reported for school use; they do not establish when this use first arose relative to learning.
A bronze-inscription example concerns archery instruction. The evidence does not establish a full semantic sequence from learning to teaching.
The phrase 成學 is reported with the meaning “complete one’s studies”; it illustrates a contextual use of 學.

senses.gloss: feel; perceive, written with the graph 學
senses.text: A Han-slip use has 學 writing 覺, “feel” or “perceive.” This is a borrowed spelling for another word, not a development of the learning meaning.

developments.text: Learning and school uses are both reported, but the examples do not show that one developed from the other or establish their relative timing.
Learning and instruction are both documented, but their chronology and any specific semantic transition are not established.

limitations.text: Period-separated examples do not establish a complete chronology or every link among learning, school, instruction, imitation, and knowledge.
The reported Han use of 學 for 覺 has no earlier occurrence or complete sound history documented here.
